source_text: Σκοπῶμεν δὲ οὕτως. Εἰ πᾶσα ἀπιστία μὴ προχείρως καὶ κατά τινα δόξαν ἄκριτον ἐγγινομένη τισίν, ἀλλὰ μετά τινος αἰτίας ἰσχυρᾶς καὶ τῆς κατὰ τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἀσφαλείας· τότε γὰρ τὸν εἰκότα σώζει λόγον, ὅταν αὐτὸ τὸ πρᾶγμα περὶ οὗ ἀπιστοῦσιν ἄπιστον εἶναι δοκῇ· τὸ γάρ τοι τοῖς οὐκ οὖσιν ἀπίστοις ἀπιστεῖν ἀνθρώπων ἔργον οὐχ ὑγιαινούσῃ κρίσει περὶ τὴν ἀλήθειαν χρωμένων. Οὐκοῦν χρὴ καὶ τοὺς περὶ τῆς ἀναστάσεως ἀπιστοῦντας ἢ διαποροῦντας μὴ πρὸς τὸ δοκοῦν αὐτοῖς ἀκρίτως καὶ τὸ τοῖς ἀκολάστοις κεχαρισμένον τὴν περὶ ταύτης ἐκφέρειν γνώμην, ἀλλ᾿ ἢ μηδεμιᾶς αἰτίας ἐξάπτειν τὴν τῶν ἀνθρώπων γένεσιν (ὃ δὴ καὶ λίαν ἐστὶν εὐεξέλεγκτον), ἢ τῷ θεῷ τὴν τῶν ὄντων ἀνατιθέντας αἰτίαν εἰς τὴν τοῦδε τοῦ δόγματος ἀποβλέπειν ὑπόθεσιν, καὶ διὰ ταύτης δεικνύναι τὴν ἀνάστασιν οὐδαμόθεν ἔχουσαν τὸ πιστόν. Τοῦτο δὲ ποιήσουσιν, ἐὰν δεῖξαι δυνηθῶσιν ἢ ἀδύνατον ὂν τῷ θεῷ ἢ ἀβούλητον τὰ νεκρωθέντα τῶν σωμάτων ἢ καὶ πάντη διαλυθέντα πάλιν ἑνῶσαι καὶ συναγαγεῖν πρὸς τὴν τῶν αὐτῶν ἀνθρώπων σύστασιν. Ἐὰν δὲ τοῦτο μὴ δύνωνται, παυσάσθωσαν τῆς ἀθέου ταύτης ἀπιστίας καὶ τοῦ βλασφημεῖν ἃ μὴ θέμις· ὅτι γὰρ οὔτε τὸ ἀδύνατον λέγοντες ἀληθεύουσιν οὔτε τὸ ἀβούλητον, ἐκ τῶν ῥηθησομένων γενήσεται φανερόν. Τὸ ἀδύνατόν τινι γινώσκεται κατ᾿ ἀλήθειαν τοιοῦτον ἢ ἐκ τοῦ μὴ γινώσκειν τὸ γενησόμενον, ἢ ἐκ τοῦ δύναμιν ἀρκοῦσαν μὴ ἔχειν πρὸς τὸ ποιῆσαι καλῶς τὸ ἐγνωσμένον. Ὅ τε γὰρ ἀγνοῶν τι τῶν γενέσθαι δεόντων οὐκ ἂν οὔτ᾿ ἐγειρῆσαι οὔτε ποιῆσαι τὸ παράπαν δυνηθείη ὅπερ ἀγνοεῖ· ὅ τε γινώσκων καλῶς τὸ ποιηθησόμενον, καὶ πόθεν γένοιτ᾿ ἂν καὶ πῶς, δύναμιν δὲ ἢ μηδ᾿ ὅλως ἔχων πρὸς τὸ ποιῆσαι τὸ γινωσκόμενον ἢ μὴ ἀρκοῦσαν ἔχων, οὐκ ἂν ἐγχειρήσειε τὴν ἀρχήν, εἰ σωφρονοίη καὶ τὴν ἰδίαν ἐπισκέψαιτο δύναμιν, ἐγχειρήσας δὲ ἀπερισκέπτως οὐκ ἂν ἐπιτελέσειε τὸ δόξαν. Ἀλλ᾿ οὔτε ἀγνοεῖν τὸν θεὸν δυνατὸν τῶν ἀναστησομένων σωμάτων τὴν φύσιν κατά τε μέρος ὅλον καὶ μόριον, οὔτε μὴν ὅποι χωρεῖ τῶν λυομένων ἕκαστον, καὶ ποῖον τῶν στοιχείων μέρος δέδεκται τὸ λυθὲν καὶ χωρῆσαν πρὸς τὸ συγγενές, κἂν πάνυ παρ᾿ ἀνθρώποις ἀδιάκριτον εἶναι δοκῇ τὸ τῷ παντὶ πάλιν προσφυῶς ἡνωμένον. Ὧι γὰρ οὐκ ἠγνόητο πρὸ τῆς οἰκείας ἑκάστου συστάσεως οὔτε τῶν γενησομένων στοιχείων ἡ φύσις ἐξ ὧν τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων σώματα, οὔτε τὰ μέρη τούτων ἐξ ὧν ἤμελλεν λήψεσθαι τὸ δόξαν πρὸς τὴν τοῦ ἀνθρωπείου σώματος σύστασιν, εὔδηλον ὡς οὐδὲ μετὰ τὸ διαλυθῆναι τὸ πᾶν ἀγνοηθήσεται ποῦ κεχώρηκεν ἕκαστον ὧν εἴληφε πρὸς τὴν ἑκάστου συμπλήρωσιν. Ὅσον μὲν γὰρ κατὰ τὴν νῦν κρατοῦσαν παρ᾿ ἡμῖν τῶν πραγμάτων τάξιν καὶ τὴν ἐφ᾿ ἑτέρων κρίσιν, μεῖζον τὸ τὰ μὴ γενόμενα προγινώσκειν· ὅσον δὲ πρὸς τὴν ἀξίαν τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ τὴν τούτου σοφίαν, ἀμφότερα κατὰ φύσιν, καὶ ῥᾴδιον ἐπ᾿ ἴσης τῷ τὰ μὴ γενόμενα προγινώσκειν τὸ καὶ διαλυθέντα γινώσκειν.
orientation: Athenagoras is laying down the standard that critics of the resurrection must meet if their disbelief is to be reasonable.
pass_a_gloss: Let us consider it in this way. If all disbelief does not come to some people readily and according to some uncritical opinion, but with some strong cause and with the certainty that accords with the truth; for then it preserves the reasonable account, whenever the very matter about which they disbelieve seems to be unbelievable; for indeed to disbelieve things that are not unbelievable is the work of human beings who do not use sound judgment about the truth. Therefore it is necessary that also those who disbelieve or are perplexed about the resurrection should not bring forward their opinion about it according to what seems good to them uncritically and what is pleasing to the undisciplined, but either to attach the origin of human beings to no cause at all (which indeed is very easy to refute), or, attributing the cause of the things that exist to God, to look to the foundation of this doctrine, and through this to show that the resurrection has its credibility from nowhere. And they will do this, if they are able to show either that it is impossible for God or unwilled by God to unite again and gather together the bodies that have died or even been completely dissolved, toward the constitution of the same human beings. But if they cannot do this, let them cease from this godless disbelief and from blaspheming what is not lawful; for that neither those who say it is impossible nor those who say it is unwilled speak the truth, will become clear from what will be said. The impossible for someone is known in truth to be such either from not knowing what will come to be, or from not having sufficient power to do well what has been known. For the one who is ignorant of something of the things that must come to be could neither undertake nor do at all what he is ignorant of; and the one who knows well what is to be made, and from where and how it would come to be, but either has no power at all to do what is known or does not have sufficient power, would not attempt it in the first place, if he were prudent and examined his own power, and if he attempted it without due consideration he would not complete what seemed good. But it is not possible that God is ignorant of the nature of the bodies that will be raised, both as a whole and part by part, nor indeed where each of the things that are dissolved goes, and which part of the elements has received what was dissolved and gone to what is akin to it, even if what has been united again naturally to the whole seems to human beings to be entirely indistinguishable. For the one for whom before the proper constitution of each thing neither the nature of the elements that would come to be, from which the bodies of human beings come, was unknown, nor the parts of these from which he was going to take what seemed good for the constitution of the human body, it is quite clear that not even after the whole has been dissolved will it be unknown where each of the things he took for the completion of each thing has gone. For as far as concerns the order of things that now prevails among us and the judgment based on other things, it is greater to foreknow the things that have not come to be; but as far as concerns the worth of God and his wisdom, both are according to nature, and it is equally easy to know the things that have been dissolved as to foreknow the things that have not come to be.

choices.english: with the certainty that accords with the truth
choices.why: ἀσφάλεια here means firmness or certainty of reasoning, and the phrase ties it to truth, not to personal confidence.
σώζειν τὸν λόγον is idiomatic for maintaining a rational position; 'reasonable account' keeps the logical force.
The term denotes those lacking moral self-control; 'undisciplined' captures the ethical sense without modernizing.

choices.term: τὴν τοῦδε τοῦ δόγματος ἀποβλέπειν ὑπόθεσιν
choices.english: to look to the foundation of this doctrine
choices.why: ὑπόθεσις here means the underlying basis or premise; 'foundation' fits the argumentative context.
rejected: to look to the hypothesis of this doctrine
to consider the subject of this doctrine

choices.why: The adjective is passive in force, meaning 'not willed'; adding 'by God' clarifies the agent from context.

choices.term: πρὸς τὴν τῶν αὐτῶν ἀνθρώπων σύστασιν
choices.english: toward the constitution of the same human beings
choices.why: σύστασις is the technical term for the composition or standing-together of the whole person; 'constitution' preserves the philosophical register.
rejected: for the formation of the same humans
for the establishment of the same people

pass_b_english: Let us consider the matter this way. If any disbelief arises in people not hastily or from some unexamined opinion, but only when it comes with a strong cause and with the certainty that accords with the truth does it preserve the reasonable account—namely, when the very thing disbelieved appears to be unbelievable. For to disbelieve things that are not unbelievable is the work of people who are not using sound judgment about the truth. Therefore those who disbelieve or are perplexed about the resurrection must not declare their opinion about it hastily, according to what merely seems right to them and what pleases the undisciplined. They must either attach no cause at all to the origin of human beings—which is very easy to refute—or, if they attribute the cause of existing things to God, they must look to the foundation of this doctrine and show through it that the resurrection has no credibility anywhere. They will do this if they can demonstrate that it is either impossible for God or unwilled by God to unite again and gather together bodies that have died or been completely dissolved, toward the constitution of the same human beings. If they cannot do this, let them cease from this godless disbelief and from blaspheming what is not right. For it will become clear from what follows that they are not speaking the truth when they say it is impossible or unwilled.

A thing is known to be truly impossible for someone either because he does not know what is going to happen, or because he does not have sufficient power to accomplish well what he knows. For someone who is ignorant of something that must happen could neither raise up nor accomplish at all what he does not know. And someone who knows well what is to be done, and knows from what source and how it could come about, but either has no power at all to do what he knows or does not have sufficient power, would not attempt it in the first place if he were prudent and examined his own power; and if he attempted it recklessly, he would not complete what he had decided.

But it is not possible for God to be ignorant of the nature of the bodies that will be raised, in whole and in every part, nor of where each of the dissolved things goes, and which part of the elements has received what was dissolved and moved toward what is akin to it—even if what has been naturally united again to the whole seems entirely indistinguishable to human beings. For the one who was not ignorant before each thing's own constitution—neither of the nature of the elements that would come to be, from which human bodies are made, nor of the parts of these elements from which he was going to take what seemed good for the constitution of the human body—clearly will not be ignorant after the whole has been dissolved of where each of the things he took for the completion of each body has gone. For as far as concerns the order of things now prevailing among us and our judgment about other things, it is greater to know in advance things that have not yet come to be; but as far as concerns the worth of God and his wisdom, both are natural, and it is equally easy for him to know things that have been dissolved as to know in advance things that have not yet come to be.

problems.source_quote: Εἰ πᾶσα ἀπιστία μὴ προχείρως καὶ κατά τινα δόξαν ἄκριτον ἐγγινομένη τισίν
problems.why: The source uses a conditional 'If' (Εἰ) to set up a hypothetical case, not a negative statement 'Not every'.
problems.fix: Let us consider the matter this way. If any disbelief arises in people not hastily or from some unexamined opinion,
problems.ruling: Εἰ πᾶσα...μὴ is conditional 'If all...not', not 'Not every'—changes logical structure from hypothetical to categorical.

problems.why: Glossary requires 'purpose' for γνώμη, but here ἀκολάστοις means 'licentious/intemperate', not 'undisciplined' in a way that violates glossary. However, checking: the glossary term is γνώμη=purpose. This is ἀκολάστοις. No glossary violation. Wait—re-checking: the issue is 'opinion' for γνώμη. The glossary fixes γνώμη as 'purpose', but the English has 'declare their opinion' for 'τὴν περὶ ταύτης ἐκφέρειν γνώμην'. 'Opinion' is not the fixed glossary term 'purpose'.
problems.ruling: γνώμη glossed as 'purpose' but rendered 'opinion' in 'τὴν περὶ ταύτης ἐκφέρειν γνώμην'; glossary violation
